name: uring-sync
baseline: cp -r (read/write syscalls); rsync over SSH for network
workload: Local copy of 100K x 100KB and 100K x 4KB files on NVMe, cold cache; and 9.7GB laptop-to-GCP transfer with kTLS.
claimed_speedup: 4.2x faster than cp -r (5.4s vs 22.7s, 100K x 100KB); 1.5x on 100K x 4KB (5.14s vs 7.67s); 3.2x on GCP pd-standard (19s vs 60s); 58% faster than rsync over network (165s vs 390s, 9.7GB).
hardware: Local NVMe on an unnamed Ubuntu laptop (CPU model not stated); GCP pd-standard VM
tradeoffs: Linux-only (io_uring, splice, kTLS need recent kernels); copy-tool, not a general library; single worker with deep queue design.
caveats: First-party numbers; CPU model and compiler flags not stated; baseline is cp -r, not a raw read/write or io_uring baseline; speedup depends on many-small-file workloads (only 1.5x on 4KB files); splice mode measured slower than read/send in its own docs.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN: File copier 4x faster than cp using io_uring' (item 46543759); repo located via WebSearch (dev.to post blocked)

name: wcp
workload: Copying 20 x 512MiB, 7,000 x 1MiB and 200,000 x 1KiB files on a Samsung NVMe SSD.
claimed_speedup: 20x512MiB: 3.97s (2579.59 MiB/s) vs cp 8.44s (1213.38 MiB/s); 7000x1MiB: 2.64s vs cp 8.29s; 200000x1KiB: 3.92s vs cp 9.23s (README says up to 70% faster).
hardware: 64GB RAM, Samsung NVMe SSD (exact model and CPU not stated)
tradeoffs: Linux-only (io_uring via vendored liburing); experimental; copies files only with progress bar.
caveats: README itself calls it experimental and possibly not robust; cache state and filesystem not stated; no compiler flags or CPU model; language taken from repo layout (src/, CMake, liburing), may include C++.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN: wcp' (item 26375565) surfaced via search 'Show HN: File copier 4x faster than cp using io_uring github'

name: lsr
baseline: GNU ls 9.7 (readdir/stat syscalls); also eza, lsd, uutils, busybox
workload: Listing a directory of n plain files (10 to 10,000) with ls -al, timed with hyperfine, syscalls counted with strace -c.
claimed_speedup: n=10,000: lsr 22.1 ms vs ls 38.0 ms (about 70% faster), busybox 32.5 ms, eza 40.2 ms; 848 syscalls vs 30,396 for GNU ls.
compiler_and_flags: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall (install instruction; benchmark build flags not explicit)
tradeoffs: Linux io_uring benefit only; on macOS/BSD no syscall batching; Zig 0.15.1 build; ls clone (not a library, not callable from C++ as an API); HN thread raised security concerns about io_uring.
caveats: First-party; CPU/hardware not stated; not an io_uring-vs-read/write library comparison but a tool comparison; the 70% figure is at 10,000 files only and smaller directories narrow the gap.

name: bfs
workload: Traversing a home directory of about 7.6 million files with the -false expression (traversal only), timed with hyperfine and tailfin.
claimed_speedup: bfs 3.0.1 about 2.91x faster than GNU find and 3.40x faster than fd, 2.20x faster than bfs 2.6.3 (snippet only).
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; packaged in Debian, Arch, Fedora, Alpine
tradeoffs: find-compatible CLI, not a library; uses io_uring and parallel traversal on Linux; breadth-first order.
caveats: Snippet only: the blog post with the numbers is egress-blocked here, and the repo README/docs carry no numbers; numbers come from WebSearch snippet of the author's blog; hardware and flags unknown.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Bfs 3.0: The Fastest Find Yet' (item 36783449) and 'lsr' thread comments mentioning io_uring traversal

name: fcp (Svetlitski)
workload: Copying the Linux kernel source tree and 13 x 512MB files on SSD (AWS EC2 a1.metal XFS; 2018 MacBook Pro APFS).
claimed_speedup: Linux: about 10x faster on kernel source (675 ms vs 6.02 s), about 1.4x on 13x512MB files (8 s vs 11.3 s); macOS about 6x and about 822x (copy-on-write).
hardware: AWS EC2 a1.metal (16 CPUs, 32GB, XFS); 2018 MacBook Pro (i9, 16GB, APFS)
tradeoffs: Parallel directory walk and copy; poor on HDD; subset of cp options; Rust CLI.
caveats: First-party; exact timing figures are from a WebSearch summary of the README table (README fetch showed only ratios), verify before use; macOS 822x is copy-on-write clone, not a data-copy speedup; a1.metal is Arm.

name: hop
workload: Reading individual files out of an uncompressed archive of the tigerbeetle repository.
claimed_speedup: 25x faster than unzip and 10x faster than tar at reading individual files (uncompressed).
hardware: macOS 12 (M1X) and an Ubuntu AMD64 server (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Archive format with no compression, no checksums, 4 GB limit, read-only, single-threaded.
caveats: No license found in the page; HN commenters note the right baseline is asar (indexed archive) not tar/unzip; early-stage 3-hour project; not a filesystem or IO baseline from the category list.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Hop: Faster than unzip and tar at reading individual files' (item 29178710)
